_notes: Chronology: dates follow a ministry from the Baptism c. AD 29 (Luke 3:1, as in data.js) to the Crucifixion in April AD 33, with Passovers in AD 30 (John 2), 31, 32 (John 6) and 33. Robertson himself dated the Crucifixion AD 30 or 29; the order of events is his either way.

Lanes: uses `women` (§169 spices, §171 emptytomb: the women's visits to the tomb) and `apostles` (§172 peterjohn: Peter and John at the tomb). §175 guardreport uses `rome` (the soldiers' report and bribe).
New place `jerusalem` (Jerusalem, place not recorded; certainty Traditional) for §182, the appearance to James, whose place Paul does not give.
§177 (appearance to Simon): the place of the appearance itself is not given; the event is mapped at `upperroom`, where the news was told (Luke 24:33).
Gospels keys include `1Cor` (§177, §179, §181, §182) and `Acts` (§183, §184), following Robertson.

Journeys in this batch (Emmaus and back, to Galilee and back) are the disciples' walks; the risen Jesus appears rather than travels. Route for §183 starts at galileemount though §182 is at `jerusalem`.

caiaphas.name: House of Caiaphas
caiaphas.note: The high priest's palace stood in the wealthy Upper City. Two traditions compete: the Armenian site on Mount Zion near the Cenacle, and the Church of St Peter in Gallicantu on the eastern slope of Zion, built in 1931 over rock-cut cellars.

emmaus.name: Emmaus
emmaus.note: Luke places Emmaus about seven miles (60 stadia) from Jerusalem; some early manuscripts read 160 stadia, about 19 miles. Emmaus Nicopolis (Imwas, near Latrun), honored since the 3rd and 4th centuries by Eusebius and Jerome, fits the longer figure. Abu Ghosh, el-Qubeibeh (a Crusader-era tradition kept by the Franciscans) and Motza (the Emmaus of Josephus, about 4 miles out) are the other candidates. The map marks Nicopolis.

galileemount.name: The mountain in Galilee
galileemount.note: Matthew 28:16 says only "the mountain to which Jesus had directed them" and gives no name. Some traditions point to Mount Tabor, others to Mount Arbel above the Sea of Galilee or to the hill of the Beatitudes. The map marks the hills west of the lake as a general location.

jerusalem.name: Jerusalem (place not recorded)
jerusalem.note: Used for events the New Testament places in no definite spot. St Paul records an appearance to James (1 Corinthians 15:7) but says nothing of where or when. A tradition from the lost Gospel of the Hebrews, quoted by St Jerome, places it in Jerusalem soon after the Resurrection.

olives.name: Mount of Olives
olives.note: The ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, about 2,700 ft high. Constantine built the Eleona church over a cave near the summit; the Pater Noster church there today recalls the teaching of the Lord's Prayer.

tabgha.name: Tabgha (Sea of Galilee shore)
tabgha.note: Heptapegon, "seven springs," about 2 miles west of Capernaum. Warm springs flow into the lake here and draw fish, so fishermen have long worked this shore. Nearby is a small bay, often called the Bay of Parables, whose slope forms a natural amphitheater: a voice from a boat carries to a crowd on the shore.

tomb.name: The Tomb (Holy Sepulchre)
tomb.note: John says the tomb was new, in a garden near the place of crucifixion. The rock-cut tomb honored since the 4th century lies a few dozen yards west of Calvary inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, under the small shrine called the Edicule; other 1st-century tombs survive in the same quarry. The Garden Tomb near Gordon's Calvary is a peaceful place of prayer, but archaeologists date it to the Iron Age, centuries before Jesus.

upperroom.name: Upper Room (Cenacle)
upperroom.note: The Gospels name only "a large upper room furnished" in the city. Since at least the 4th century, Christians have honored a site on Mount Zion, in the southwest of the old city, as the room of the Last Supper and of Pentecost. The present Gothic hall was built by the Crusaders and Franciscans in the 12th to 14th centuries. Robertson suggests it may have been the house of John Mark's mother (Acts 12:12).

events.title: The women watch the tomb and buy spices
events.summary: The women who had followed Jesus from Galilee rested on the Sabbath, as the Law required. Late on the Sabbath they went to look at the tomb. When the Sabbath ended at sundown, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Salome bought spices so they could anoint his body at first light. They expected to find a dead man.

scripture.text: And when the sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him.
Now after the sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the sepulchre.

events.orderNote: Matthew 28:1 can be read "late on the sabbath" (Robertson, following the King James sense) or "after the sabbath, toward the dawn" (RSV). Robertson takes it as a Saturday-evening visit to see the tomb, before the Sunday-morning visit of §171; many others read it as the same Sunday visit.

Mt.text: Now after the sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the sepulchre.

Mk.text: And when the sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him.

events.title: The earthquake and the angel at the tomb
events.summary: Before sunrise on the first day of the week there is a great earthquake. An angel of the Lord comes down, rolls back the stone and sits on it. The guards set at the tomb shake with fear and become like dead men. No Gospel describes the moment of the Resurrection itself: the stone is rolled away not to let Jesus out, but to let the witnesses see that the tomb is empty.

scripture.text: And behold, there was a great earthquake; for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven and came and rolled back the stone, and sat upon it.
His appearance was like lightning, and his raiment white as snow. And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men.

art.title: The Resurrection
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Christ stands with one foot on the edge of the tomb, holding a banner and looking straight out at us, while four soldiers sleep below.
art.significance: Painted for the town hall of Sansepolcro, whose name means "Holy Sepulchre."
art.symbolism: The landscape is bare on the left and in leaf on the right: winter turns to spring. One sleeping soldier is traditionally said to be Piero's self-portrait.
art.impact: Aldous Huxley called it "the best picture in the world" (1925); the story goes that a British officer spared the town from shelling in 1944 because of it.

art.title: The Angel Seated on the Stone of the Tomb
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: A pale, almost transparent angel in white fills the doorway of the tomb, beside the empty burial shelf where the grave cloths lie.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: Tissot paints the angel in white on gray, light dissolving into light, to suggest "raiment white as snow."
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: Robertson counts the days in the Jewish way: part of Friday, all of Saturday and the early hours of Sunday make "the third day." Only Matthew tells of the guard, the earthquake and the angel on the stone.

events.title: The women find the tomb empty
events.summary: At early dawn the women come with their spices, wondering who will roll away the large stone. They find it already rolled back and the body gone. An angel (Luke and John speak of two) tells them, "He has risen, he is not here," and sends them to tell the disciples, and Peter, that Jesus is going before them to Galilee. The first witnesses of the empty tomb are women.

scripture.text: and as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, "Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen.
And he said to them, "Do not be amazed; you seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen, he is not here; see the place where they laid him.
But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you."

echoes.note: "On the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him."

art.title: Resurrection of Christ and Women at the Tomb
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: An angel seated on the open tomb points upward to the risen Christ in a mandorla of light, unseen by the women who peer into the empty tomb. St Dominic kneels at the left.
art.significance: Painted for a friar's cell, as an aid to prayer; St Dominic kneels at the side as a model of contemplation.
art.symbolism: The women look into the empty tomb and do not yet see Christ above them: the viewer sees what they will soon believe.
art.impact: The San Marco cell frescoes are among the most loved devotional images of the Italian Renaissance.

art.title: Mary Magdalene and the Holy Women at the Tomb
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: The women shrink back at the tomb door: inside stands a shining angel beside the folded grave cloths, while the guards lie sprawled on the ground like dead men.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: The red lanterns of the night watch still hang by the door, but the light now comes from inside the tomb.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: The four accounts differ in detail: one angel (Matthew, Mark) or two (Luke, John), "while it was still dark" (John) or "when the sun had risen" (Mark). Many harmonists take John 20:1 to mean that Mary Magdalene came first, in the dark, saw the stone moved and ran back to Peter (§172) while the others went on.

Mt.text: So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.

Mk.text: And they went out and fled from the tomb; for trembling and astonishment had come upon them; and they said nothing to any one, for they were afraid.

Lk.text: and as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, "Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen.

Jn.text: Now on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb.

events.title: Peter and John at the empty tomb
events.summary: Mary Magdalene runs to Simon Peter and the beloved disciple: "They have taken the Lord out of the tomb." The women's report seems to the apostles an idle tale. Peter and the other disciple run to the tomb. The younger disciple arrives first and looks in; Peter goes inside and sees the linen cloths lying, and the head cloth rolled up by itself. The beloved disciple then goes in, and "he saw and believed."

scripture.text: They both ran, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first;
Then the other disciple, who reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed; for as yet they did not know the scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.

echoes.note: "You do not give me up to Sheol, or let your godly one see the Pit": the scripture St Peter later cites for the Resurrection (Acts 2:27).

art.title: The Disciples Peter and John Running to the Sepulchre on the Morning of the Resurrection
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Peter and the young John run side by side at dawn, their faces full of hope and fear.
art.significance: Shown at the Paris Salon of 1898 and bought by the French state.
art.symbolism: Everything is in the faces and the wind-blown hair: we see not the tomb but the race toward it.
art.impact: Widely reproduced as one of the best-known Easter images of the modern era.

art.title: Saint Peter and Saint John Run to the Sepulchre
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: The young John, in white, reaches the low tomb door first; the older Peter runs behind him, outside the city wall.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: Tissot follows John's detail that the other disciple outran Peter; the city wall behind shows the tomb lay outside Jerusalem.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: Some ancient manuscripts omit Luke 24:12. John's "other disciple, whom Jesus loved" is traditionally identified as John son of Zebedee.

Lk.text: But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home wondering at what had happened.

Jn.text: Then the other disciple, who reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed;

events.title: Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene
events.summary: Mary stays at the tomb, weeping. Two angels ask why she weeps; then she turns and sees Jesus but takes him for the gardener. When he calls her by name she knows him: "Rabboni!" He tells her not to hold on to him, and sends her to his brethren. She becomes the first witness of the risen Lord, and the Church honors her as "apostle to the apostles."

scripture.text: Jesus said to her, "Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?" Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, "Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away."
Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Hebrew, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher).
Jesus said to her, "Do not hold me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brethren and say to them, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God."

echoes.note: "I sought him whom my soul loves... I held him, and would not let him go": read in the liturgy of her feast.

art.title: Resurrection (Noli me tangere)
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Two angels sit on the open tomb above the sleeping soldiers. Mary Magdalene kneels and reaches out; the risen Christ, holding a victory banner, steps away from her hands.
art.significance: One of the closing scenes of Giotto's cycle of the life of Christ in the Scrovegni Chapel.
art.symbolism: Christ's body turns away while his face and hand turn back to her: "Do not hold me." The banner with the cross is the sign of victory over death.
art.impact: The Scrovegni cycle is often called the starting point of Western Renaissance painting.

art.title: Noli me tangere
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Mary Magdalene kneels in a Venetian landscape and reaches toward Christ, who draws back his robe, a gardener's hoe in his hand.
art.significance: An early masterpiece of Titian, painted when he was in his twenties.
art.symbolism: The hoe recalls that Mary took him for the gardener; the tree and farm buildings link Easter to the renewal of the earth.
art.impact: One of the best-loved Venetian paintings in London, bequeathed by the poet Samuel Rogers in 1856.

events.orderNote: Mark 16:9 says he appeared "first" to Mary Magdalene, and Robertson counts this the first of five appearances on Easter Day. Mark 16:9–20, the longer ending of Mark, is missing from many early manuscripts, including the two oldest complete Greek Bibles (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus); the Church receives it as inspired, canonical Scripture.

Mk.text: Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.

Jn.text: Jesus said to her, "Mary." She turned and said to him in Hebrew, "Rabboni!" (which means Teacher).

events.title: Jesus meets the other women
events.summary: As the women hurry from the tomb with fear and great joy, Jesus meets them with a greeting. They take hold of his feet and worship him. He tells them not to be afraid, and to tell his brethren to go to Galilee, where they will see him. Even after the Passion, he still calls the disciples who fled "my brethren."

scripture.text: And behold, Jesus met them and said, "Hail!" And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him.
Then Jesus said to them, "Do not be afraid; go and tell my brethren to go to Galilee, and there they will see me."

art.title: Jesus Appears to the Holy Women
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: The risen Jesus, in shining white among olive trees, raises his hand in greeting as the women come toward him along the path.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: The women have not yet seen him: Tissot paints the moment just before they fall at his feet and worship him.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: Matthew names Mary Magdalene and "the other Mary." Robertson treats this as a separate appearance to the other women, after the one to Mary Magdalene alone in John; others take Matthew's account as a shorter telling of the same meeting.

events.title: The guard's report and the bribe
events.summary: While the women are on their way, some of the guard go into the city and tell the chief priests everything that has happened. The priests and elders take counsel and pay the soldiers to say that the disciples stole the body while they slept. They promise to protect them if the governor hears of it. Matthew notes that this story was still told among the Jews in his own day.

scripture.text: And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sum of money to the soldiers and said, "Tell people, 'His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.'
So they took the money and did as they were directed; and this story has been spread among the Jews to this day.

events.orderNote: Matthew does not say where the priests met; the map uses the high priest's house. Robertson calls the guard "Roman watchers"; Pilate's "You have a guard" (Matthew 27:65) can also be read as "take your own Temple guard," though the fear of the governor in 28:14 suggests Roman soldiers.

events.title: The road to Emmaus
events.summary: That afternoon two disciples, one named Cleopas, walk from Jerusalem to the village of Emmaus, talking sadly about all that has happened. Jesus joins them, but they do not recognize him. Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he explains how the Christ had to suffer and enter his glory. At table he takes bread, blesses and breaks it, and their eyes are opened; then he vanishes. Luke's words echo the Last Supper and the Eucharist.
events.stay: The two pressed him to stay with them for the night, "for it is toward evening."
events.journey: Luke says about 7 miles (60 stadia) from Jerusalem; if Emmaus is Nicopolis, as some manuscripts (160 stadia) and early tradition suggest, about 19 miles west along the road toward the coastal plain.

scripture.text: And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed, and broke it, and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened and they recognized him; and he vanished out of their sight.
They said to each other, "Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the scriptures?"

echoes.note: The suffering servant, "wounded for our transgressions": the heart of "Moses and all the prophets" read as pointing to the Christ.
"Then the eyes of both were opened": the Fathers saw the eyes opened at Emmaus as undoing the first eating.

art.title: Supper at Emmaus
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: A beardless young Christ blesses the bread. One disciple grips the arms of his chair, the other flings his arms wide, while the innkeeper looks on, unaware.
art.significance: Painted in Rome for the nobleman Ciriaco Mattei, at the height of Caravaggio's early fame.
art.symbolism: The basket of fruit teeters at the table's edge, as if into our space; Christ's unfamiliar face recalls that their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
art.impact: One of the most famous moments of recognition in Western art, and a model for Baroque realism.

art.title: The Supper at Emmaus
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: In a bare, high stone room, Christ breaks the bread with a soft light around his head, while the two disciples begin to understand.
art.significance: A late Rembrandt, quiet where Caravaggio is dramatic.
art.symbolism: The great niche behind Christ works like an apse, so that the simple supper becomes an altar.
art.impact: Admired as one of the most inward religious paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.

events.orderNote: The site of Emmaus is disputed: Nicopolis, Abu Ghosh, el-Qubeibeh and Motza all have advocates (see the place note). Mark 16:12–13 tells the same appearance briefly; Mark 16:9–20, the longer ending of Mark, is missing from many early manuscripts, including the two oldest complete Greek Bibles (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus); the Church receives it as inspired, canonical Scripture.

Mk.text: After this he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country.

Lk.text: When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed, and broke it, and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened and they recognized him; and he vanished out of their sight.

events.title: "He has appeared to Simon!"
events.summary: The two from Emmaus get up that same hour and go back to Jerusalem. Before they can speak, the eleven and those with them greet them with the news: "The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!" Then the two tell how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. The appearance to Peter alone is never described; St Paul lists it first among the witnesses he hands on.
events.journey: The two disciples walked back to Jerusalem the same evening, about 7 miles by Luke's figure (about 19 if Emmaus is Nicopolis).

scripture.text: And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem; and they found the eleven gathered together and those who were with them, who said, "The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!"
Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.

art.title: Apparition of Our Lord to Saint Peter
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Among olive trees, Peter, in a dark cloak, stops short as he sees Jesus in white beside a tree. Tissot imagines the appearance to Peter alone, which the Gospels mention but never describe.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: Peter, who had denied him three times, is the first of the apostles to see the risen Lord.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: Neither Luke nor Paul says where or exactly when Jesus appeared to Simon Peter, only that it was on Easter Day, before the evening gathering. The map places the event where the news was told, the room where the eleven were gathered, traditionally the Upper Room.

events.title: Jesus appears to the disciples (Thomas absent)
events.summary: That evening, with the doors shut for fear, Jesus stands among the disciples and says, "Peace be with you." They think they see a spirit, so he shows them his hands, feet and side, and eats a piece of broiled fish before them. He sends them as the Father sent him, breathes on them and gives them the Holy Spirit and the power to forgive sins. Thomas is not there, and refuses to believe unless he can touch the wounds.

scripture.text: See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; handle me, and see; for a spirit has not flesh and bones as you see that I have."
Jesus said to them again, "Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you." And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit.
If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained."

echoes.note: God breathed into man the breath of life; the risen Christ breathes on his disciples, a new creation.

art.title: The Appearance of Christ at the Cenacle
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus, in glowing white, stands among the disciples in a dim pillared room; they bow low or shrink back in fear.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: Tissot sets the scene in the Cenacle, following the tradition that the disciples gathered where they had eaten the Last Supper.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

art.title: Christ Appears to the Apostles at Table
art.medium: Tempera on panel
art.description: The risen Christ enters from the left and greets the apostles seated around a table under arches; dishes of fish lie on the cloth.
art.significance: From the back of the Maestà, Siena Cathedral's high altarpiece.
art.symbolism: Mark says he appeared "as they sat at table"; Luke adds that he ate fish before them.
art.impact: The Maestà was carried in procession to the cathedral in 1311, and is a cornerstone of Sienese painting.

events.orderNote: Robertson counts this the first of three commissions to the apostles (with §181 and §183). The Church sees in John 20:22–23 the institution of the sacrament of Penance (Council of Trent). Mark 16:14 tells it briefly; Mark 16:9–20, the longer ending of Mark, is missing from many early manuscripts, including the two oldest complete Greek Bibles (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus); the Church receives it as inspired, canonical Scripture.

Mk.text: Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they sat at table; and he upbraided them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.

Lk.text: They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.

Jn.text: And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, "Receive the Holy Spirit.

events.title: Doubting Thomas: "My Lord and my God!"
events.summary: Eight days later the disciples are again indoors, and this time Thomas is with them. Jesus comes and stands among them, and invites Thomas to put his finger in the wounds. Thomas makes the fullest confession of faith in the Gospels: "My Lord and my God!" Jesus blesses all who believe without seeing. John adds that he wrote so that readers may believe and have life in his name.
events.stay: The disciples were still in Jerusalem a week later; Robertson thinks Jesus stayed at or near the city this first week, then went to Galilee.

scripture.text: Then he said to Thomas, "Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side; do not be faithless, but believing."
Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!" Jesus said to him, "Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe."
but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

art.title: The Incredulity of Saint Thomas
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Christ guides Thomas's hand so that his finger enters the wound in his side, as two other apostles lean in to look.
art.significance: One of Caravaggio's most copied works in his own century.
art.symbolism: The four heads form a tight cross around the wound; Thomas's furrowed brow shows doubt giving way to faith.
art.impact: Its blunt physical realism made it one of the defining images of this Gospel scene.

art.title: The Disbelief of Saint Thomas
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Thomas kneels and bows his head to the risen Jesus' hand, while the other disciples crowd around in the shadows.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: The wounds remain in the glorified body: the risen Christ is the same one who was crucified.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: Robertson links this appearance to Paul's "then to the twelve" (1 Corinthians 15:5). John 20:30–31 reads like the original close of the Gospel, so many scholars see chapter 21 as an epilogue.

events.title: Breakfast by the sea and the great catch
events.summary: Back in Galilee, seven disciples go fishing with Peter on the Sea of Tiberias and catch nothing all night. At daybreak a stranger on the shore tells them to cast the net on the right side, and it fills with 153 large fish. The beloved disciple says, "It is the Lord!" and Peter throws himself into the sea. Jesus has a charcoal fire ready, and gives them bread and fish. It is his third appearance to the disciples in John.
events.journey: The disciples went back to Galilee as Jesus had told them, about 100 miles, 4 to 5 days on foot, probably down the Jordan Valley.

scripture.text: He said to them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." So they cast it, and now they were not able to haul it in, for the quantity of fish.
That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, "It is the Lord!" When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his clothes, for he was stripped for work, and sprang into the sea.
Jesus said to them, "Come and have breakfast." Now none of the disciples dared ask him, "Who are you?" They knew it was the Lord.

echoes.note: Fishermen stand beside a river flowing from the Temple, with fish "of very many kinds." St Jerome linked the 153 fish to every kind of fish then known.

art.title: The Miraculous Draught of Fishes
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Christ, in a red cloak, stands at the water's edge while the disciples haul in the net and Peter swims toward him.
art.significance: Part of an altarpiece for St Peter's Cathedral in Geneva.
art.symbolism: Witz sets the scene on Lake Geneva, with the Mont Salève behind, bringing the Gospel into his viewers' own world.
art.impact: Often called the first recognizable landscape in European painting.

art.title: Meal of Our Lord and the Apostles
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: At dawn on the shore of the lake, Jesus and the disciples sit around a charcoal fire, with loaves on the ground and the boat drawn up behind.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: The thin column of smoke from the fire recalls John's detail of "a charcoal fire there, with fish lying on it, and bread."
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: Robertson notes the exact date is unknown, only that it falls between Easter Day and the Ascension. It closely echoes the first miraculous catch when Peter was called (Luke 5:1–11). The traditional site is Tabgha, but John names only the Sea of Tiberias.

events.title: "Feed my sheep": Peter restored
events.summary: After breakfast Jesus asks Peter three times, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Three times Peter, who had denied him three times beside a charcoal fire, says yes, and three times Jesus gives him charge of his flock. He foretells that Peter will one day stretch out his hands and die for him, and says again, "Follow me." The Catholic Church reads this as the confirmation of Peter's pastoral primacy.

scripture.text: When they had finished breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" He said to him, "Yes, Lord; you know that I love you." He said to him, "Feed my lambs."

He said to him the third time, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" Peter was grieved because he said to him the third time, "Do you love me?" And he said to him, "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you." Jesus said to him, "Feed my sheep.

Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you girded yourself and walked where you would; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go." (This he said to show by what death he was to glorify God.) And after this he said to him, "Follow me."

echoes.note: God himself will seek out his sheep and feed them; now Christ entrusts that work to Peter.

art.title: Christ's Charge to Peter
art.medium: Bodycolour on paper mounted on canvas (tapestry cartoon)
art.location: Victoria and Albert Museum, London (Royal Collection)
art.description: On a lakeside meadow Christ points to a flock of sheep while Peter kneels before him with the keys; the other apostles crowd behind.
art.significance: One of the full-size designs Raphael made for tapestries commissioned by Pope Leo X for the Sistine Chapel.
art.symbolism: The keys (Matthew 16:19) and the sheep (John 21) are joined in one image of Peter's charge as shepherd of the Church.
art.impact: The cartoons were bought by Charles I in 1623 and are among the treasures of the Royal Collection.

art.title: Feed My Lambs
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: On the stony lake shore Jesus lays his hand on Peter's shoulder and speaks with him; other disciples follow behind.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: The threefold question answers Peter's threefold denial.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: The saying about the beloved disciple (21:23) shows a rumor in the early Church that he would not die. Tradition holds that Peter was crucified in Rome under Nero, about AD 64–67.

events.title: The Great Commission on the mountain in Galilee
events.summary: The eleven go to the mountain in Galilee where Jesus told them to meet him. When they see him they worship, though some doubt. He declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him, and sends them to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. He promises to be with them always, to the close of the age.
events.journey: From the lake shore up into the Galilean hills, perhaps about 5 to 10 miles; the mountain is not named.

scripture.text: And Jesus came and said to them, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, to the close of the age."
Then he appeared to more than five hundred brethren at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep.

echoes.note: The one like a son of man receives dominion over "all peoples, nations, and languages."

art.title: Christ Appears to the Disciples on the Mountain in Galilee
art.medium: Tempera on panel
art.description: The eleven stand together on a bare, rocky slope as Christ, in dark blue and gold, speaks to them with open hands.
art.significance: From the back of the Maestà, Siena Cathedral's great high altarpiece, which ends with the appearances after the Resurrection.
art.symbolism: The gold ground lifts the mountain out of time: this is the commission to all nations.
art.impact: The Maestà was carried in procession to the cathedral in 1311, and is a cornerstone of Sienese painting.

events.orderNote: Robertson thinks the appearance to "more than five hundred brethren" (1 Corinthians 15:6) was most probably this appointed meeting, and reckons Mark's commission the same as Matthew's; others place Mark 16:15–18 in Jerusalem. Mark 16:9–20, the longer ending of Mark, is missing from many early manuscripts, including the two oldest complete Greek Bibles (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus); the Church receives it as inspired, canonical Scripture.

Mt.text: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

Mk.text: And he said to them, "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to the whole creation.

events.title: Jesus appears to James
people: James, the brother of the Lord
events.summary: St Paul records, in a single line, that the risen Lord "appeared to James, then to all the apostles." This James, called the brother of the Lord, had not believed in Jesus during the ministry (John 7:5). Soon after he is with the apostles and the women in the Upper Room (Acts 1:14), and later he leads the church in Jerusalem. Paul met him there about three years after his own conversion (Galatians 1:19).

scripture.text: Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

art.title: Saint James the Less
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: A bearded man in white kneels on a rock with his arms flung wide in prayer, part of Tissot's series of the apostles.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, says James the Just prayed so much that his knees grew hard like a camel's. Western tradition often identifies James the Less with James the brother of the Lord; the identification is debated.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: No place or time is given. A tradition from the Gospel of the Hebrews, quoted by St Jerome, places the appearance in Jerusalem; the map follows it, as a tradition only. Catholic tradition holds that the "brethren" of the Lord were his kinsmen, not sons of Mary, and often identifies this James with James son of Alphaeus, "the Less."

events.date: End of the forty days, AD 33
events.title: "You shall be my witnesses"
events.summary: Back in Jerusalem near the end of the forty days, Jesus opens the disciples' minds to understand the scriptures: the Christ must suffer and rise on the third day, and repentance and forgiveness of sins must be preached to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. He tells them to stay in the city until they are clothed with power from on high. When they ask about the kingdom of Israel, he promises the Holy Spirit and sends them to be his witnesses to the end of the earth.
events.stay: Acts says he appeared to them during forty days, speaking of the kingdom of God and eating with them.
events.journey: The disciples returned from Galilee to Jerusalem before the end of the forty days, about 90 to 100 miles, probably by the Jordan Valley.

scripture.text: and said to them, "Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
And behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you; but stay in the city, until you are clothed with power from on high."
But you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth."

echoes.note: "I will pour out my spirit on all flesh": the promise of the Father, fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–17).
"A light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth."

art.title: Jesus Discourses with His Disciples
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus, in white, walks along a hillside road with a group of disciples, talking with them as they go.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: The walking teacher and his listeners suit Luke's summary of the forty days: he opened their minds to understand the scriptures and spoke of the kingdom of God.
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: Read alone, Luke 24 seems to put this teaching on Easter evening; Acts 1:3 shows Luke knew of forty days of appearances. Robertson, like many harmonists, places Luke 24:44–49 at the end of the forty days as the third commission.

events.title: The Ascension
events.summary: Jesus leads the disciples out toward Bethany on the Mount of Olives. He lifts up his hands and blesses them, and as they watch he is lifted up, and a cloud takes him out of their sight. Two men in white promise that he will come again in the same way. The disciples return to Jerusalem with great joy, praising God in the Temple and waiting for the Spirit.
events.journey: From the city across the Kidron Valley and up the Mount of Olives, about a mile, "a sabbath day's journey" (Acts 1:12).

scripture.text: Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.
And when he had said this, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.
and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."

echoes.note: Elijah is taken up into heaven before Elisha's eyes, who then receives a double share of his spirit.
"Sit at my right hand": Mark says the Lord "sat down at the right hand of God."

art.title: Ascension
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Christ rises on a cloud between two hosts of angels and saints, his hands reaching past the top of the frame. Below, Mary and the apostles kneel, and two angels in white point upward.
art.significance: The scene follows the Noli me tangere in Giotto's life of Christ in the Scrovegni Chapel.
art.symbolism: Christ's hands already touch the edge of the picture, as if entering heaven beyond it; the two angels in white are the "two men" of Acts 1:10.
art.impact: The Scrovegni cycle is often called the starting point of Western Renaissance painting.

art.title: The Ascension
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Christ rises above the Mount of Olives, his arms spread in blessing, as the disciples look up from below.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's Life of Christ, 350 watercolors made after his return to the Church and three study trips to Palestine (1886–1896).
art.symbolism: The raised hands follow Luke: "lifting up his hands he blessed them... and was carried up into heaven."
art.impact: Exhibited in Paris, London and New York in the 1890s, the series drew huge crowds; the Brooklyn Museum bought all 350 in 1900.

events.orderNote: Luke 24:50 says he led them "as far as Bethany," Acts 1:12 says Olivet; Bethany lies on the far slope of the same hill, and the traditional site is near the summit. The Church keeps the feast forty days after Easter. Mark 16:19–20 also tells it; Mark 16:9–20, the longer ending of Mark, is missing from many early manuscripts, including the two oldest complete Greek Bibles (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus); the Church receives it as inspired, canonical Scripture.

Mk.text: So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God.

Lk.text: And they worshiped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.
